A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FP64/PINN study. Their text, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A-D are readable and matchable; v2 adds computational-cost results and a checklist without material comparison gaps.

before.justification: v1 reports original PINN experiments, including loss-landscape analyses, precision sweeps and performance comparisons on four PDE problems in Sections 4-5.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and additionally reports FP32/FP64 runtime and memory measurements in Table 2.

M1.justification: The FP64 training approach, vanilla PINN architecture, residual objective and L-BFGS optimization procedure are unchanged. The new computational-cost evaluation introduces no method component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate convection, reaction, wave and Allen-Cahn equations, retaining the same PDE conditions and convection-parameter sweep. The new resource measurements reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains PINN, QRes, PINNsFormer, KAN, PirateNet, RoPINN and PINNMamba as comparators to PINN_FP64, including the missing RoPINN Allen-Cahn results. Figure 8 also retains its original comparator membership.

E3.justification: Table 2 introduces efficiency evaluation using training seconds per iteration and GPU memory in MB for FP32 and FP64 on an H100 PCIe. Existing accuracy metrics, the 101x101 collocation grid, model configurations and PDE settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.5 adds an analysis of the runtime and memory overhead of increasing precision across the four retained PDEs. Existing initialization, loss-landscape, training-dynamics, optimizer-stopping and precision-sensitivity analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: The new checklist's item 7 describes Table 1's existing uncertainty quantities as confidence intervals; v1 did not identify their type. Their values are unchanged, and v2 supplies no confidence level, calculation method or evidence of additional runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds runtime and memory results: for example, convection uses 0.29 s/iteration and 1609 MB with FP32 versus 0.32 s/iteration and 2441 MB with FP64. Table 1 and the existing figures retain their results; Table 2's rRMSE values repeat Table 1.

T1.justification: Equations 1-16, including the PDE definitions, machine-precision discussion and Appendix B's L-BFGS formulas, are unchanged. No new mathematical result, derivation or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about precision-induced optimization stalls, a shared loss basin, three training phases and FP64 as the remedy. The computational-cost addition does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.5 newly characterizes FP64 overhead as marginal on modern GPUs, invoking H100 Tensor Core throughput and suggesting larger memory accesses explain the latency increase. Appendix D's limitations are unchanged, while the checklist adds that any GPU supporting double precision can run the experiments.

D1.justification: v2 adds measured time and memory requirements and specifies H100 PCIe hardware. The checklist also recommends A100/H100 GPUs and discloses use of PINNMamba code with stated CC-BY 4.0 and MIT licenses; the original code link and software settings are unchanged.

R1.justification: The same 37 references and substantive related-work positioning are retained, including the contrast with loss-barrier explanations and low-precision practices in mainstream deep learning.

P1.justification: v2 adds the short Section 5.5, acknowledgements and a NeurIPS checklist, and updates the conference footer. Existing prose, section order and Appendices A-D are otherwise essentially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 2 and adjusts spacing and float placement: Table 1 moves from page 7 to page 8, and Figure 7 joins Figure 8 on page 9. Existing figures and Table 1 retain their visual content and organization.

improvement.justification: v1 discusses FP64's resource drawbacks qualitatively; v2's Table 2 and Section 5.5 quantify runtime and memory overhead, making practical tradeoffs easier to assess. This is a limited improvement: measurements cover one GPU and per-iteration costs, so they do not establish total training or energy costs or substantiate the broader overhead claim across hardware.
